content.thinking:
I need to be careful in the postmortem not to restate figures as if I computed them myself. The ClientDisconnected errors look like pre-existing background noise rather than a real signal, and the actual symptom is the p99 latency spike from around 200ms to 1338ms, which deserves an explicit assumption note.

A prior incident tried reverting the monthly-spend-feature without recovery, and there's a confusing log where Argus refused to act before pivoting to the flag candidate anyway — worth flagging as an assumption. The 24h deploy query found nothing but an 8-minute window turned up one production change, likely the flag toggle itself, and recovery timing correlates with but doesn't prove the revert caused the fix. I'll write the root cause around the flag ramp-up triggering the latency regression with flat volume, errors, and memory, then draft an executive summary avoiding specific component names where possible.

I'm now compiling the list of assumptions: the causal link between the revert and recovery is weak given the prior incident's failed revert, the error rate bump may just be background noise since latency was the real signal, the identified production change is unverified as the flag flip, the internal mechanism of the slow code path was never pinpointed, and only this service's telemetry was reviewed with no downstream dependency data.

I'm also being careful to keep the log coverage window (08:52–09:26) and the unreviewed draft PR noted, without restating the given impact figures as if I'd computed them myself — I'll frame the recovery window as measured/reported rather than calculated, and make sure not to conflate Argus hold time with actual outage duration.

assumptions: Recovery is attributed to the flag revert on correlation alone: the service was back at baseline roughly 30 seconds after the revert and the responder marked the action CONFIRMED, but no controlled re-test was done. This is weakened by the record that reverting the same flag on an earlier incident (f1339376-4294-4407-a6d6-073275df155c) did not produce a recovery, which is why the responder had initially pushed this action down its list.

The incident is characterised as a latency fault, not an error fault. The ClientDisconnected errors on the account page appear continuously in the logs from 08:52 onward at levels comparable to (and at times higher than) those during the incident window, so the measured rise above baseline may reflect normal variance in that pre-existing noise rather than new failures caused by the flag.

The 24-hour deploy query returned no production changes, while a query over the 8 minutes before 09:30 returned one. That change was not described in the evidence; it is assumed to be the flag flip itself rather than a code or config release. If it was a release, the root cause above would need revisiting.

Only io-shop's own metrics and logs were examined. No telemetry from any downstream or upstream dependency was pulled, so the alternative reading — that the new code path calls an already-slow dependency and the flag merely exposed it — was neither confirmed nor excluded. Under that reading the flag is the trigger, not the underlying fault.
Log evidence covers 08:52-09:26 only. Behaviour after 09:26, including the recovery, was judged from metrics rather than logs.
Resource exhaustion was ruled out from memory staying in its usual band against a 2 GiB limit and an unchanged process start time; no host- or container-level telemetry beyond these was inspected.
The draft pull request opened at 09:38 is assumed to address the slow code path. It has not been reviewed, tested or merged, so the service is currently protected only by the flag being off.
The 0.02 hours the responder held the incident is a response-time measure and is not the duration of customer impact; impact ran 09:22 to 09:28.
input.executive_summary: Shoppers viewing their account page saw it load very slowly — worst-case page responses went from a fifth of a second to well over a second — starting at 09:22 UTC on 24 September 2026 and clearing at 09:28 UTC, roughly six minutes of degradation as recorded by the metrics. Pages generally still loaded; the small rise in outright failures over the window is reported separately in the incident's impact figures, and it sits within the range of page errors the service was already seeing before the incident began. The cause was a newly enabled feature on the account page, switched on minutes earlier; no software release was involved. The automated responder detected the alert, identified the change, and switched the feature back off, after which response times returned to their normal level. A draft code fix has been opened for the slow path and is not yet reviewed or merged. The feature remains off in the meantime.
input.root_cause: The `monthly-spend-feature` flag was switched on for io-shop — ramping at 09:21 and fully on at 09:22 — which enabled an account-page code path whose p99 latency jumped from roughly 200ms to ~1338ms in the same minute and stayed elevated until the flag was reverted. No code or config deployment had occurred in the preceding 24 hours, and request volume, error rate and memory were flat across the shift, so the flag flip is the only change that lines up with the onset; the specific work the new path performs (the investigator's speculative "slow spend-aggregation query" reading) was never identified.
